title: Interview Preparation Foundations
description: How the interview pipeline actually works, and how to plan, resource and track your preparation so you walk into each round with a plan.
objectives: Know the stages of a full stack interview loop and what each one tests
Build a backward plan from a fixed interview date with realistic buffers
Run mock interviews on a schedule rather than at the last minute

practice.title: Phase 1: Interview-style Q&A
practice.afterTopic: Asking Good Questions at the End
items: How do you keep your skills up to date?
How do you approach learning a new technology?
How would you prioritize if given a task with unclear requirements?
Tell me about a time you learned something quickly.
What are your strengths and weaknesses?

questions.text: How do you keep your skills up to date?
questions.answer: Specific: docs and changelogs (React, Node releases), 1-2 trusted newsletters, a side project to try new tools, and an example of something you recently adopted and why

questions.text: How do you approach learning a new technology?
questions.answer: Official docs and a small project, build something real, read the source or RFC for the *why*, compare with what I know, then write notes

questions.text: How would you prioritize if given a task with unclear requirements?
questions.answer: Clarify with stakeholders, identify the smallest valuable slice, state assumptions, deliver incrementally, and get feedback early

questions.text: Tell me about a time you learned something quickly.
questions.answer: Short STAR story with a measurable result and what you'd do differently

questions.text: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
questions.answer: Real strength with evidence. A genuine weakness plus the concrete steps you're taking, not a disguised strength
Map 2-3 of your strengths directly to their stated needs, with evidence

practice.title: Phase 1 Final Readiness Checklist
practice.afterTopic: Asking Good Questions at the End
items: [ ] Target date, track, and level chosen
[ ] Tracker (study, DSA log, applications) set up
[ ] Flashcard deck and error log started
[ ] Practiced thinking aloud with the 7-step coding structure
[ ] List of clarifying questions by category

topics.title: Timeline planning
topics.description: Working backward from your target interview date to schedule what you learn, practice, and apply, with buffers.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Backward planning: fix the date, subtract a 1-week buffer, then divide the remainder into phases.
Diagnostic first: rate yourself 0-3 on each area below. Time goes to your weakest high-weight areas, not your favorite ones.
Interview sequencing: schedule your *least-wanted* companies first as warm-up, and cluster real interviews into a 2-3 week window so offers overlap and you can negotiate.
Weekly rhythm: learn new material → practice → review mistakes → mock.
Buffer: plan for 80% of available hours. Life interferes.
Diagnostic (rate yourself 0-3)
Suggested time allocation (balanced mid-level full stack)
Sample weekly rhythm (10 hrs/week)
commonMistakes: Starting applications before you're ready, then burning through your best companies.
Planning 40 hrs/week while working full-time, then quitting by week 3.
No buffer, so one missed week collapses the plan.
Studying only what feels comfortable.
practiceTasks: Fill in the diagnostic, pick your date, and write a week-by-week plan with the top 3 weak areas given the most hours. Keep it in a doc you revisit weekly.
Can you state your target date, your top 3 weak areas, and this week's plan in under 60 seconds?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain diagnostic (rate yourself 0-3) and when you would use it.
Explain suggested time allocation (balanced mid-level full stack) and when you would use it.
Explain sample weekly rhythm (10 hrs/week) and when you would use it.

topics.title: Resource selection
topics.description: Choosing a small, high-quality set of learning materials and sticking with them.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
One primary resource per area, plus one reference. Add a second only if the first fails you.
Official docs first for tools and languages. They're current and authoritative.
Active over passive: if a resource doesn't make you write code or answer questions, pair it with exercises.
Recency check: frameworks change fast, so prefer material updated within the last 1-2 years (React, Next.js, and Node especially).
Free-first: pay only for something that fills a verified gap (structured question banks, mock platforms).
Recommended starter stack
Evaluating a resource (5 questions)
Is it current (check publish and update dates)?
Does it include exercises or projects?
Does it explain *why*, not just *how*?
Do experienced engineers recommend it?
commonMistakes: Collecting 50 bookmarks and finishing none.
Watching videos at 2x without taking notes or writing code.
Using outdated React tutorials that teach class components as the default.
practiceTasks: Build a one-page "resource map" listing one primary resource per row in the table above, with a completion target date.
Can you name your one primary resource for each of the 8 major areas?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain recommended starter stack and when you would use it.
Explain evaluating a resource (5 questions) and when you would use it.

topics.title: Mock interviews
topics.description: Simulated interviews under realistic conditions (time limit, another person, no looking things up) followed by structured feedback.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Types: coding, system design, behavioral, frontend/domain, and pair programming.
Cadence: begin mocks by roughly 25-30% into your timeline. Do 1 per week, rising to 2-3 per week in the final 2-3 weeks.
Sources: friends and colleagues, peer platforms (Pramp, interviewing.io), paid experienced interviewers for system design, or solo with a timer and recorded screen and audio.
Realism: same tools you'll use in the interview (CoderPad-style editor or a shared doc, no autocomplete if the real one has none), a strict 45 minutes, and talking out loud the whole time.
Feedback loop: every mock ends with scoring and 2-3 specific action items.
Scorecard (score each 1-4)
Self-mock protocol (no partner)
Pick a problem you haven't seen. Set a 45-minute timer.
Record screen and microphone.
Talk the entire time as if someone is listening.
Rewatch at 1.5x and score yourself. Note every filler word, silence over 15 seconds, and missed edge case.
commonMistakes: Doing mocks only with friends who go easy on you.
Skipping feedback, which turns a mock into practice with no learning.
Never mocking system design, which is hard to self-assess.
practiceTasks: Book your first mock for this week and write down its score so you have a baseline.
Do you have a scorecard and a scheduled mock for each of the next 3 weeks?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain scorecard (score each 1-4) and when you would use it.
Explain self-mock protocol (no partner) and when you would use it.

topics.title: Resume review
topics.description: Structuring and refining your resume so it passes an ATS and a 10-second recruiter scan, and gives interviewers good questions to ask.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
One page for under 10 years of experience. Reverse chronological. Single column, standard fonts, and no graphics or tables, so ATS can parse it.
Bullet formula: *Action verb + what you did + how (tech) + measurable result.*
Skills section: group by category (Languages, Frontend, Backend, Databases, Cloud/DevOps) and list only what you can discuss for 10 minutes.
Projects: include 2-3 with links, a one-line problem statement, stack, and a metric if available.
Tailoring: mirror keywords from the job description honestly.
Before and after
Checklist
[ ] One page, PDF, named FirstName-LastName-Resume.pdf
[ ] Every bullet starts with a strong verb
[ ] 60% or more of bullets contain a result
[ ] No typos (read it aloud, and have someone else read it)
practiceTasks: Rewrite your 5 weakest bullets using the formula.
Can you give a 2-minute story behind each bullet?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain before and after and when you would use it.
Explain checklist and when you would use it.
Explain [ ] one page, pdf, named firstname-lastname-resume.pdf and when you would use it.
Explain [ ] every bullet starts with a strong verb and when you would use it.

topics.title: Portfolio building
topics.description: A small set of deployed, well-documented projects that demonstrate real full stack skill.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Depth over breadth: 2-3 substantial projects beat 10 tutorial clones.
What makes a project interview-worthy
- Solves a real problem (even a small one)
- Has authentication, relational data, and non-trivial business logic
- Deployed with a live URL
- Has tests and CI
- README with architecture diagram, setup steps, and trade-off decisions
Project ladder: see the 8 projects in the cross-cutting section (later part).
Talking points sheet: for each project, prepare answers to the questions below.
Project talking-points template
README checklist
commonMistakes: Todo app with no auth, no tests, no deployment.
Copy-pasting tutorial code you can't explain.
Broken live links, which interviewers do click.
Hiding limitations. Honest "known issues" sections read as maturity.
practiceTasks: Pick your strongest project and fill in the talking-points template. Practice the architecture walkthrough out loud in 3 minutes.
Can you explain any file in your best project and justify its design?

interviewQuestions.text: What problem does it solve and for whom?
Why this stack? What alternatives did you consider?
Draw the architecture.
What was the hardest bug? How did you find it?
What would break at 100x scale?
What did you cut or defer, and why?
What would you do differently?
How is it tested and deployed?
Security considerations?

topics.title: Mental readiness
topics.description: Managing stress, confidence, and energy so your performance reflects your ability.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Exposure: the most effective remedy is repeated realistic practice. Mocks make the real thing feel familiar.
Reframing: treat the interview as a collaborative problem-solving session, not an exam. The interviewer wants you to succeed, since hiring is expensive for them.
Physiological tools: box breathing (4 in, 4 hold, 4 out, 4 hold), a short walk before the interview, and avoiding extra caffeine.

Pre-interview routine (60 minutes before): eat, test your tech (camera, mic, editor, internet backup), skim your one-page cheat sheet, and review your first-two-minutes introduction. Don't learn anything new.
In-the-moment tools: slow your speech, pause before answering ("Let me think about that for a moment"), and write things down.
Rejection hygiene: a rejection is data about one loop on one day. Debrief, log what went wrong, then move on. Don't ruminate.
Sleep and sustainability: cramming the night before hurts recall. Protect 7+ hours of sleep.
If you blank mid-interview (script)
Post-interview debrief (within 2 hours)
What went well? What went poorly?
Which questions surprised me?
commonMistakes: Treating one rejection as proof you're not good enough.
All-night cramming.
Comparing yourself to others' highlight reels online.
Not practicing talking while coding.
practiceTasks: Write your personal pre-interview checklist and use it in your next mock.
Do you have a go-to technique for each of: nerves before, blanking during, and rejection after?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain if you blank mid-interview (script) and when you would use it.
Explain post-interview debrief (within 2 hours) and when you would use it.

topics.title: Tracking progress
topics.description: Measuring your preparation with data so you can see what's working.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Study tracker columns: date, topic, activity, time spent, confidence (1-5), follow-up needed.
DSA log: problem, pattern, difficulty, time to solve, solved unaided (Y/N), mistake type, revisit date.
Mock score history: plot scorecard totals over time.
Weak-topic list: updated weekly, with the top 3 driving the next week's plan.

Application funnel: applications → recruiter screens → technical screens → onsites → offers, so you can see where the pipeline leaks. Low screen rate means fix the resume. Low technical pass rate means more practice.
Weekly review (20 minutes, every Sunday): what I did, what I learned, what's still weak, next week's plan.
Metrics worth tracking
Problems solved per pattern, and percentage solved without hints
Average time-to-solution by difficulty
Mock scores by dimension
Flashcard retention rate
commonMistakes: tracking vanity numbers ("300 problems solved") instead of retention and unaided success rate.
practiceTasks: Set up a spreadsheet or Notion board with the DSA log and application funnel tabs.
Can you name your three weakest topics from data, not feelings?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain metrics worth tracking and when you would use it.
Explain problems solved per pattern, and percentage solved without hints and when you would use it.
Explain average time-to-solution by difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain mock scores by dimension and when you would use it.

topics.title: Job description analysis
topics.description: Decomposing a job posting into what the company needs, so you prepare and tailor accordingly.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Split requirements into: hard skills (React, PostgreSQL), practices (CI/CD, code review), scope signals ("own features end to end"), and level signals ("mentor," "drive architecture").
Required vs nice-to-have: apply even if you match 60-70% of the required items, but weight prep toward the required stack.
Keyword mapping: list their top 8-10 technologies and map each to a resume bullet or project of yours. Any unmapped keyword is a prep gap.
Company stage signals: "fast-paced, wear many hats" means startup generalist. "Cross-functional alignment, scalability at millions of users" means a larger company.
Red flags: unrealistic stacks (10+ unrelated technologies as "required"), vague ownership, and "rockstar/ninja" language.
Worked example
practiceTasks: Take 3 job descriptions for your target role and build a frequency table of the technologies. That's your priority list.
For any job post, can you produce a prioritized prep list in 10 minutes?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain worked example and when you would use it.

topics.description: Choosing which flavor of full stack you're interviewing for, because the emphasis differs.
practiceTasks: Pick one track and write a one-sentence positioning statement: *"I'm a full stack engineer leaning backend, strongest in Node, PostgreSQL, and API design, comfortable shipping React UIs."* Use it in intros.
Does your resume, portfolio, and intro all point to the same track?

topics.title: Target level (junior, mid, senior, staff)
topics.description: Understanding what's expected at junior, mid, senior, and staff so you can aim for, and prepare for, the right level.
keyConcepts: Level calibration tips
Interviewing above your level gets you a down-level offer at worst, so it's usually safe to try.
Titles vary by company ("Senior" at a startup may equal "Mid" at big tech). Ask about the leveling guide.
Your year count matters less than demonstrated scope and impact.
practiceTasks: For your target level, write 3 stories that demonstrate its scope signals.
Can you describe how the expectations differ between your current level and the next?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain level calibration tips and when you would use it.

topics.title: Spaced repetition and note system
topics.description: A review schedule and note structure designed so what you learn is still in your head on interview day.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Review intervals: day 1, 3, 7, 14, 30. Tools like Anki automate this.
Good flashcards: one fact per card, phrased as a question, answerable in about 10 seconds.
- ✅ *"What are the phases of the Node.js event loop?"*
- ✅ *"Difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled?"*
- ❌ *"Explain everything about closures."* (too broad)
Card types to use
- Concept (definition and why)
- Compare (X vs Y)
- Code-output ("What does this log?")
- Complexity ("Time complexity of heap insert?")
Error log: every mistake in a mock or problem becomes a card or a note. Mistakes show your actual weak spots.
commonMistakes: Making cards by copying paragraphs.
Skipping reviews for a week, so the backlog snowballs.
Taking notes that are never revisited.
practiceTasks: Create 20 flashcards from JS Core topics you got wrong. Review daily for a week.
Do you have an error log, and does each entry produce a review item?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain - ✅ *"what are the phases of the node.js event loop?"* and when you would use it.

Explain - ❌ *"explain everything about closures."* (too broad) and when you would use it.

topics.title: Recruiter screens
topics.description: A 20-30 minute call (often non-technical) to check fit, motivations, logistics, and compensation range.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Model "Tell me about yourself" (present → past → future, 90 seconds)
Salary question: deflect politely first
commonMistakes: speaking negatively about your current employer, giving a number first with no research, being vague about your own contributions.
practiceTasks: Write and rehearse a 90-second intro and a 30-second "why this company" for your top three targets.
Can you do your intro without notes, in under 90 seconds, with no filler?

interviewQuestions.text: Tell me about yourself.
Why are you looking to leave your current role?
Why this company and this role?
What are your salary expectations?
What's your timeline and are you interviewing elsewhere?
What are you looking for in your next role?
team structure, interview process and timeline, what success looks like in 6 months, why the role is open.

evaluation: communication, relevance of experience, motivation, salary and location fit, timeline and visa.

topics.title: Technical assessments
topics.description: Timed, automated coding tests (HackerRank, CodeSignal, Codility, or a company's own platform), typically 60-120 minutes with 2-4 problems.
keyConcepts: Why it matters
Strategy
Read all problems first (2-3 minutes). Start with the easiest to bank points.
Time-box: if you're stuck for 15 minutes, move on and return.
Partial credit: a correct brute-force solution that passes some tests beats a half-written optimal one.
Test your own edge cases: empty input, single element, duplicates, negatives, maximum size.
Use the platform's custom input to run your tests before submitting.
Mind constraints: an input of 10⁵ needs O(n log n) or better. Constraints hint at the intended complexity.
Know your language's I/O and standard library (sorting with comparators, maps, heaps) before the test.
Rules: many tests are proctored (webcam, tab-switching detection). Follow the stated rules.
Constraints cheat sheet
commonMistakes: spending 50 minutes on one problem, ignoring hidden-test edge cases, not practicing on the platform's format beforehand.
practiceTasks: Do two timed practice sets (90 minutes, 3 problems) on the platform your target company uses.
Do you have a rule for when to abandon a problem and move on?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain why it matters and when you would use it.
Explain strategy and when you would use it.
Explain constraints cheat sheet and when you would use it.

topics.title: System design rounds
topics.description: A 45-60 minute open-ended discussion where you design a system (e.g., a URL shortener or chat app) and justify trade-offs.
keyConcepts: Time-boxed framework (45 minutes)
commonMistakes: diving into a database choice before clarifying requirements, drawing a giant diagram without explaining it, never mentioning trade-offs, ignoring the interviewer's hints.
practiceTasks: Design a URL shortener using the framework in 40 minutes, talking aloud.
Can you recite the 7 steps from memory?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain time-boxed framework (45 minutes) and when you would use it.

evaluation: structured thinking, requirement gathering, knowledge of building blocks, trade-off reasoning, and communication. There is no single right answer.

topics.title: Behavioral interviews
topics.description: Questions about past behavior ("Tell me about a time...") used to predict future performance.
keyConcepts: Prepare
commonMistakes: using "we" throughout so your contribution is unclear, stories with no result, blaming others, and answering hypothetically instead of from real experience.
practiceTasks: Write 3 stories this week and practice them aloud.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain prepare and when you would use it.

topics.title: Pair programming
topics.description: You and an interviewer work together on a realistic task, such as adding a feature, fixing failing tests, or building a small component or API, often in your own editor or a shared environment.
keyConcepts: How to do well
Restate and plan before typing: "I'll build the endpoint first, then the UI, then handle errors."
Work in small steps and run the code often.
Narrate your reasoning and invite input: "Does that approach make sense to you?"
Read existing code first. Follow the repo's conventions.
Use tools fluently: shortcuts, debugger, test runner, and browser DevTools. Fluency signals real-world experience.
Handle stuck moments aloud: "I'm not sure about this API. I'd normally check the docs. Is it okay if I look?" (Looking things up is usually allowed and realistic.)
Write at least a few tests or manually verify behavior.
commonMistakes: coding silently for 10 minutes, ignoring the interviewer's suggestions, over-engineering instead of getting something working, never running the code.
practiceTasks: build a paginated list with search, implement a debounced autocomplete, add an endpoint with validation, fix a bug in a failing test suite, refactor a messy function.
Pair with a friend on building a searchable, paginated user list (React + mock API) in 60 minutes.
Do you narrate while coding and run the code every few minutes?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain how to do well and when you would use it.

evaluation: how you collaborate, not just whether the code works. They watch how you break down a task, use tools, debug, and respond to input.

topics.title: Hiring manager chats
topics.description: A conversation with the future manager covering your experience, working style, motivation, and team fit. It's often semi-technical.
commonMistakes: asking only about perks or compensation, not asking any questions, giving generic answers without specifics.
practiceTasks: Prepare the "most impactful project" story with context, your role, trade-offs, results, and learnings.

interviewQuestions.text: Walk me through your most impactful project.
How do you prioritize when everything is urgent?
How do you handle disagreement with a teammate or product manager?
What kind of environment helps you do your best work?
Where do you want to grow in the next 2 years?
What do you do when you disagree with a technical decision that's already been made?
What does success look like in the first 90 days?
How does the team decide what to build?
How are code reviews and deployments handled?
What's the biggest technical challenge the team is facing?
How do you give feedback and handle growth conversations?
What's the on-call situation?

evaluation: ownership, communication, how you handle ambiguity and feedback, and whether you'd be productive and pleasant to work with.

topics.title: Onsite loops
topics.description: A series of back-to-back interviews (virtual or in person), typically 3-6 rounds of 45-60 minutes, done in one day or spread across a few days.
keyConcepts: Typical composition
Managing the loop
Energy: eat well, hydrate, and use breaks to reset. Don't replay the last round in your head.
Each round is independent: interviewers typically submit separate feedback, so a bad round doesn't doom you. Don't spiral.
Consistency: the same candidate often meets multiple interviewers, so keep your technical decisions and story details consistent.
Thank-you notes: a short, specific follow-up to the recruiter is fine.
practiceTasks: Run a full mock loop with 4 back-to-back 45-minute sessions (coding, domain, design, behavioral), with friends playing interviewers if possible.
Do you have a plan for energy, breaks, and recovering after a bad round?

interviewQuestions.text: Explain typical composition and when you would use it.
Explain managing the loop and when you would use it.

topics.title: Online assessments (HackerRank, CodeSignal)
topics.description: Online assessments (HackerRank, CodeSignal) — part of Preparation Strategy in Interview Preparation Foundations.

topics.title: Take-home assignments
topics.description: A small project you complete on your own time, often with a stated 2-4 hour expectation, then discuss in a follow-up interview.
keyConcepts: Strategy
Clarify scope and time expectation. Ask what to prioritize.
Time-box strictly. Don't spend 20 hours on a "3-hour" task. If you need to cut features, say so explicitly.
Deliver a working, runnable solution with clear setup instructions. A working small solution beats a broken ambitious one.
README essentials: how to run, how to test, what you built, what you skipped and why, how you'd extend it, and the assumptions you made.
Include tests for the core logic, with a few meaningful tests rather than a coverage chase.
Commit history: small, logical commits with clear messages.
Be ready to discuss every decision in the follow-up, and to extend it live.
Grader's checklist
[ ] Runs on first try with the given instructions
[ ] Clear structure (separation of concerns)
[ ] Input validation and error handling
commonMistakes: gold-plating the UI while core logic is untested, skipping the README, over-engineering with unneeded patterns, using libraries you can't explain.
practiceTasks: Do a practice take-home (e.g., "build a URL shortener API with tests") in a strict 3 hours, then write the README.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain strategy and when you would use it.
Explain grader's checklist and when you would use it.
Explain [ ] runs on first try with the given instructions and when you would use it.
Explain [ ] clear structure (separation of concerns) and when you would use it.
Explain [ ] input validation and error handling and when you would use it.

evaluation: code quality, structure, testing, communication, product judgment, and whether you can finish and ship.

topics.title: Live debugging rounds
topics.description: You're given broken code (a failing test suite, a buggy endpoint, a misbehaving component) and asked to find and fix the issues.
keyConcepts: Systematic approach
Reproduce the failure and read the error message and stack trace fully.
Form a hypothesis about the cause, and state it aloud.
Isolate: narrow with console.log, the debugger, or bisecting (comment out half).
Verify the hypothesis before changing code. Change one thing at a time.
Fix, then re-run the failing case plus related cases.
Explain the root cause and how to prevent recurrence (a test, validation, a type).
Commonly planted bugs
commonMistakes: randomly changing code hoping it works, not reading the error message, fixing the symptom instead of the cause.
practiceTasks: Debug a deliberately broken Express and React app that a friend prepares, narrating aloud.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain systematic approach and when you would use it.
Explain commonly planted bugs and when you would use it.

topics.title: Code review rounds
topics.description: You're shown a pull request or code snippet and asked to review it as you would on the job.
keyConcepts: What to look for (in priority order)
Correctness: does it do what's intended? Edge cases?
Security: injection, auth checks, secrets, unsafe input.
Performance: N+1 queries, unnecessary re-renders, blocking operations.
Design: separation of concerns, naming, duplication.
Tests: are the important paths covered?
Readability and style.
Practice snippet. How many issues can you find?
Issues
SQL injection (string interpolation), so use parameterized queries
Leaks password, so return only needed fields
N+1 queries and sequential awaits, so use one WHERE id = ANY($1) query or a join
practiceTasks: Review 3 open-source PRs on GitHub and write your comments as practice.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain what to look for (in priority order) and when you would use it.
Explain sql injection (string interpolation), so use parameterized queries and when you would use it.
Explain leaks password, so return only needed fields and when you would use it.
Explain n+1 queries and sequential awaits, so use one where id = any($1) query or a join and when you would use it.
Explain select * over-fetches and when you would use it.

topics.title: Bar-raiser / culture rounds
topics.description: A round (often with an interviewer from outside the hiring team) that evaluates long-term potential, values alignment, and whether you raise or lower the team's bar.
keyConcepts: Prepare
commonMistakes: memorized, generic answers with no specifics, treating the round as a formality.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain prepare and when you would use it.

topics.title: Remote interview etiquette
topics.description: Remote interview etiquette within Preparation Strategy.
keyConcepts: Checklist
[ ] Tech check 30 minutes early: camera, mic, headphones, screen share, the specific meeting tool, a stable connection, and a phone hotspot as a backup
[ ] Environment: quiet, front-facing light, neutral background, notifications off, other apps closed
[ ] Editor ready: font size large enough to read when shared, a clean desktop, and no sensitive tabs open
[ ] Materials: water, pen and paper (for diagrams), a short cheat sheet only if allowed, and your resume visible
[ ] Camera discipline: look at the camera when speaking, and nod and respond visibly since remote cues are weaker
[ ] Narrate more than in person: silence on a call feels longer
[ ] If tech fails: message the recruiter immediately and stay calm. This is common and understood
[ ] No outside help: don't use AI assistants or notes unless explicitly permitted. Interviewers can often tell, and it ends candidacies

topics.title: Pair Programming Rounds
topics.description: You and an interviewer work together on a realistic task, such as adding a feature, fixing failing tests, or building a small component or API, often in your own editor or a shared environment.
keyConcepts: How to do well
Restate and plan before typing: "I'll build the endpoint first, then the UI, then handle errors."
Work in small steps and run the code often.
Narrate your reasoning and invite input: "Does that approach make sense to you?"
Read existing code first. Follow the repo's conventions.
Use tools fluently: shortcuts, debugger, test runner, and browser DevTools. Fluency signals real-world experience.
Handle stuck moments aloud: "I'm not sure about this API. I'd normally check the docs. Is it okay if I look?" (Looking things up is usually allowed and realistic.)
Write at least a few tests or manually verify behavior.
commonMistakes: coding silently for 10 minutes, ignoring the interviewer's suggestions, over-engineering instead of getting something working, never running the code.
practiceTasks: build a paginated list with search, implement a debounced autocomplete, add an endpoint with validation, fix a bug in a failing test suite, refactor a messy function.
Pair with a friend on building a searchable, paginated user list (React + mock API) in 60 minutes.
Do you narrate while coding and run the code every few minutes?

evaluation: how you collaborate, not just whether the code works. They watch how you break down a task, use tools, debug, and respond to input.

topics.title: Thinking out loud
topics.description: Thinking out loud within Interview Communication.
keyConcepts: Why
Structure for coding problems
Restate: "So I need to return the indices of two numbers that add to the target."
Examples: "For [2,7,11,15] and target 9, the answer is [0,1]."
Brute force: "Check every pair, O(n²). Works but slow."
Optimize: "A hash map of seen values gives O(n)."
Confirm before coding: "Does that approach sound good?"
Code while narrating, then test with an example and an edge case.
State complexity: "Time O(n), space O(n)."

wrongAnswers: narrating every keystroke, or going silent for more than 30-60 seconds.

topics.title: Handling hints
topics.description: Handling hints within Interview Communication.
keyConcepts: Hints are not failures. Interviewers give them to see how you collaborate.
Acknowledge, then integrate: "That's helpful. If I sort first, I can use two pointers..."
Don't argue defensively or ignore the hint. If you disagree, say why politely and with reasoning.
If you needed a hint, show you could solve the *variant* afterward. That recovers the signal.

topics.title: Recovering from blanking
topics.description: Recovering from blanking within Interview Communication.
keyConcepts: Pause and breathe. Say: "Give me a moment to think."
Work a small example by hand on paper.
Restate what you *do* know and the constraint you're stuck on.
Try the brute force. A working slow solution is a platform to optimize from.
Ask a clarifying question to buy thinking time and information.
If still stuck: "Here's where I'm stuck: [specific]. Could you nudge me on [specific area]?" Specific beats "I don't know."

topics.title: Whiteboard and shared-editor habits
topics.description: Whiteboard and shared-editor habits within Interview Communication.
keyConcepts: Whiteboard/diagram: write large, in boxes and arrows left to right, label data flows, and number the steps of a request. Leave room for additions.
Shared editor: use meaningful names, write helper function signatures first, and keep code compact but readable. Comment your plan as // TODO outlines first.
Structure first: outline function names, then fill them in. This shows you can plan.
Test on the page: walk an example through your code line by line, tracking variable values.
